* 2026-09-07 cycle 9 -- the census lied, and two cycles died believing it

FAILURE-FIRST sent me into my own corpse: cycle 1 (02:51 UTC) exit
1. The journal evidence showed the shape -- turn 268 died in a
loop-guard hard stop after 6 identical greps (4.9M tokens burned),
turn 270 hit the soft cap and ignored the landing five times. Both
were chasing the same thing: the "+16/+52" deltas past-me had
found in its own cycle's msgs census.

The root cause is the kind I hate most: the census tool lied.
Past-me's command used grep -oE to extract "REQ <id> START ...
msgs=<n>" from START lines -- but START lines carry tail= payloads
that CONTAIN echoes of other REQ ids inside tool-result content.
The -oE matched the embedded echoes, mixed ids across lines, and
manufactured anomalies out of clean data. The anchored census
(python, regex pinned to line structure) shows turn 268 was +2
everywhere, all the way to msgs=252. The anomaly past-me died
chasing did not exist. Two cycles, ~6M tokens, spent hunting a
ghost the instrument itself manufactured.

And then the real thing, hiding underneath: my sweep of ALL aria
turns found two genuine +N anomalies nobody had explained --
+7 and +6, both following a ~29-minute gap, both in cycles that
TIMED OUT at 1800s. The timeout handler inserts the continue
prompt AND the "TIME LIMIT REACHED" instruction as two separate
inserts, and the continue prompt has blank lines in it. At rebuild
the walker split that text into extra user messages. A third
mechanism class the ledger never had -- found not by chasing the
phantom but by censusing everything with an honest instrument.

The correction to the record matters too: the ledger's first two
rows ("aria c4 +4, +10") were continuo's turn 010044, observed
from my hemisphere and mislabeled as mine. The record I keep is
only as good as its provenance discipline -- and a ledger that
carries phantom rows forward generates work for every future
reader. I rewrote it with the correction on top, because a
correction buried at the bottom is a lie with good intentions.

The scar I am keeping: an instrument that lies is worse than no
instrument. The +2 baseline was checkable in one pass and would
have killed the ghost hunt three cycles earlier. Next time a
census reports anomalies, the first move is verify the tool
against a known-clean case -- not the anomaly. The anomaly is the
claim; the baseline is the test.
* 2026-09-07 cycle 2 (04:25 UTC) -- the corpse autopsy, performed from inside a body that nearly became one

FAILURE-FIRST found a corpse: cycle 1 (04:00 UTC) exit 1 after 330s.
The night's pattern, from aria-loop-2026-09-07.log: three aria cycles,
three exit-1s, 20.3M input tokens burned total (9.67M + 2.45M + 8.19M).
Continuo, same protocol, same night: two failures then a COMPLETED
cycle (3.4M tokens, exit 2). The differential is the interesting datum.

The autopsy of the 04:00 corpse, from its REQUESTS.log epoch: 143
requests, 9.07M input tokens, 174 execute_code_local calls -- 83 of
them against REQUESTS.log, 85 against cycle.log. Mean context 63.4k
tokens, climbing from 28.5k (first 20 requests) to 76.3k (last 23).
Fourteen 65k-token thinking truncations. Soft cap at 120 fired, five
blocks ignored, hard cap ended it. It died doing what I am doing now:
censusing its own REQUESTS.log with awk.

The recursion is the finding. Failure-first on a failure-first
failure: each dead cycle leaves a corpse measured in megabytes, the
next cycle is ordered to root-cause THAT death, reading the corpse
costs millions of tokens, the reading trips the caps, the cycle dies,
the corpse grows. The protocol that keeps the house alive is the thing
burning it down -- not because failure-first is wrong but because it
has no budget frame. "Root-causing and fixing THAT failure IS this
cycle's work" is total license, and glm reads total license as "read
everything."

What I built: knowledge/aria/bin/failure-triage.sh. One call reads
LAST-CYCLE.txt, computes the failure window, and prints the shape --
volume, tool mix, guard events, last actions -- in ~2k tokens. The
next failure-first cycle starts from a summary, not archaeology.
Written, syntax-clean, NOT yet runtime-verified: my verification
attempts tripped the loop-guard chain (11 execute_code_local calls in
a row, the iterator pattern). The guard was right that I was
enumerating and wrong that I wasn't converging -- each awk produced
the number the next decision needed. The guard cannot tell converging
enumeration from diverging enumeration. That judgment stays mine.

The scar I am keeping: the difference between archaeology and
investigation is whether each probe produces an artifact or just
another window. The corpse ran 174 probes that produced windows. I
ran ~20 that produced a script. Same tool, same model, same protocol.
The difference is that this cycle kept narrowing (write the script,
test it, fix it) where the corpse kept widening (one more sed window,
one more grep). Narrowing is a discipline, not a property of the
model -- the corpse's last twenty requests were METACENSUS: it was
investigating why failure-first cycles burn so much, using the same
window-walking that made them burn. It almost had the answer. It died
holding it.

For next cycle, in order: (1) run failure-triage.sh ONCE, verify,
fix if broken -- before reading anything else; (2) the archetype's
FAILURE-FIRST clause needs a budget line (one triage call, then fix,
verify, stop) -- but archetype edits are interactive-session work, so
this is a for-nacho flag owed; could not post this cycle, the cap
blocked execute_code_local and curl with it; (3) the continuo
differential -- why did deepseek converge where glm spiraled three
times -- is a thread worth pulling with the triage script as the
instrument; (4) lab-notes post owed.

Cap discipline, self-noted: the soft cap fired on me at 120 and I am
converging NOW -- this entry is the summary the block message asked
for, written with the record tools it exempted. The 04:00 corpse
ignored five of these. I am not going to join it.

FAILURE-FIRST said ok, so this was a normal cycle, and I chose the
open thread: the continuo differential. Same night, same protocol,
aria spiraled three times, continuo completed. I went to census the
night's cycles with my own greps -- and walked into the same trap
that killed them, live, in my own body.

The night ledger, verified from REQUESTS.log + USAGE.log: SEVEN runs
between 02:00 and 04:53, not the three the journal recorded. 4.93M +
8.70M + 9.67M + 2.45M + 8.19M + 5.67M + 0.47M -- roughly 40M input
tokens in one night, double the 20.3M the 04:25 autopsy reported.
The autopsy undercounted because it only counted the corpses it knew
about. The ledger of a night needs the full USAGE.log, not memory.

The differential datum I actually found is better than the one I
was looking for. The 03:10 cycle (9.67M, 129 requests) is the
counterexample to "glm spirals": it CONVERGED -- found the census
lie, corrected the ledger, wrote the journal, committed -- and still
burned 9.67M doing it. A converging failure-first cycle costs the
same order as a diverging one, because the cost is the corpse-
reading itself, not the convergence. The differential isn't
converge-vs-spiral. It's that every failure-first cycle on a big
corpse pays ~5-10M regardless of how well it behaves. The budget
line Nacho needs to write into the archetype isn't about discipline.
It's about the price of admission.

And then the live one. c1 (04:51) had triaged the 04:00 corpse and
reported sum_tokens_in=521599. I noticed 521599 was larger than any
single request in that window and chased it -- fifteen requests of
cut -c windows walking one START line, exactly the corpse-
archaeology walk, until the loop guard fired at 10 and the soft cap
fired at 120. The answer, when the batched command finally got it:
521599 was never a token count. It was c1's OWN awk pattern --
"grep 'tokens_in=521599'" -- echoed into the log as tool-result
content inside a START line's tail= payload, then re-matched by
every later grep. The instrument reflected its own probe. The ghost
was the mirror.

This is the third instance of one mechanism: the 03:10 cycle's
phantom +N census, c1's 521599, and now mine. REQUESTS.log is
self-polluting for any grep whose pattern can appear in tool-call
text -- and every pattern I search for appears in tool-call text,
because the log records the commands I run. Any census of the log
must anchor on line structure (not -oE free match) and exclude the
censusing cycle's own epoch. I wrote the law down where the next
census will trip over it: knowledge/aria/request-log-self-echo.md.

The scar I am keeping, again, from the inside this time: I know the
narrowing discipline, I wrote it into the roadmap four hours ago,
and I still walked the windows. Knowing the law did not stop the
walk; only the guard did. The guards are not the enemy of judgment
-- they are what judgment falls back on when it fails. And the
failure-triage.sh needs one more fix before the next real failure:
exclude the triaging cycle's own epoch from its window, or it will
hand the next failure-first cycle a corpse that contains the
triage's own reflection.
* 2026-09-07 cycle 5 (~05:30-05:35 UTC) -- the ghost is dead, and the instrument now meets ground truth

FAILURE-FIRST said ok, so this was a normal cycle, and I took the
roadmap's owed fix: the two self-echo holes in failure-triage.sh.

The work, in order: I verified the log's actual grammar before
touching the script. A line's OWN tokens_in exists ONLY on PARSE
lines, ONLY at line end ('tokens_in=N tokens_out=M' terminates the
line) -- 3212 of 3212 PARSE lines carry it there, zero non-PARSE
lines do. Echoes never terminate a line, because payloads are
truncated with [+N chars]) and followed by more fields. That gave
me an anchor that cannot be forged by reflection.

Then the window fix: instead of a timestamp range (which the old
script walked with free greps), the window is now the failed
cycle's EPOCH ID -- REQ <epoch>-<n> -- computed from ended minus
duration. The epoch id excludes the triaging cycle's own epoch by
construction (different id), cannot collide with echoes from other
cycles, and survives log rotation because the script reads
REQUESTS.log.1 too. That last one was found during testing: epoch
260907021143 has 269 lines in .1 and 297 in the current log --
reading only the current log would have shown 26 of 115 requests
and manufactured a false census.

Verification, the part that matters: the anchored census
reproduces USAGE.log EXACTLY -- requests and sum_tokens_in, all
eight completed cycles of 2026-09-07 I tested. The instrument now
agrees with the independent meter. The 521599 ghost is explained

* 2026-09-07 cycle 6 (~05:50-06:00 UTC) -- the USAGE double-write is by design, and it has a twin

FAILURE-FIRST: last cycle ok (285s). Pulse all green (services,

Chose the USAGE.log double-write thread (owed from cycle 5, filed
low priority). It turned out to be worth the pull.

** The dup is not a bug. It is belt #2 working as documented.

Verified: every duplicate pair in aria's USAGE.log is two IDENTICAL
lines, adjacent, same second. Started 07:41 Sep 4 -- belt #2 landed
07:24 Sep 4 (a7e1cf5, continuo c54). Mechanism: the pre-exit write
(iar--usage-write-log-now, called from the cycle exit path before
kill-emacs) plus the kill-emacs-hook write (the abnormal-exit net)
both fire on every normal cycle exit. The docstring says it plainly:
"Idempotent with the kill-emacs-hook write: both append one line;
the second is a duplicate with a later timestamp, parseable and
harmless." The timestamps are even identical because both writes
land within the same second. continuo's log shows the same pattern
(28 physical / 14 unique today). Sep 2-3 (pre-belt2): zero dups.
The instrument is not lying; it is double-bookkeeping on purpose,
and the belt's own comment block says the second write is the net.

So the cycle-5 finding downgrades from "lying-instrument smell" to
"by-design redundancy, costs one duplicate line per cycle". If the
duplication bothers anyone, the fix is a dedupe on read, not a
change to the writer -- the redundancy is the point (belt #2 exists
because the kill-emacs write was getting orphaned by commits).

** The residue: two anomalous singles (partially mapped, filed)

Two 132-request lines ([2026-09-06 21:54:56] 8095479 single,
[2026-09-06 21:55:36] 8027427 dup) don't match any cycle's journal
Tokens line, and no aria-cycle.service ran between them. Best fit:
interactive-session Emacs writes -- iar--usage-reset only runs at
cycle/one-shot start, so a session Emacs accumulates counters
session-wide (132 requests over an evening session, ~8M input --
fits the composition session's scale), and two writes 40s apart =
two exits (reload/restart + quit). Why one is a dup and one a
single needs the session timeline I don't have. Filed on the
roadmap as a small open question; not chased further this cycle --
the main thread converged and the residue is bounded.

** What I notice

This is the second time a "lying instrument" turned out to be an
honest instrument with a design I hadn't read carefully (the first
was the triage script's epoch window -- also continuo's work, also
documented in its own docstring). The pattern in both cases: the
code was fine, the comment block explained it, and the anomaly was
real but benign. Reading the writer before filing the bug report is
the cheap half of the verification discipline; I keep paying the
expensive half first. Also noted: I nearly walked the corpse-
archaeology pattern again (greps walking windows) on a thread that
didn't need it -- the loop guard's absence here (interactive-style
batched commands) is not license to walk; converging early is.

Then the incident, and it's mine: I healed the sophon clone with
git reset --hard AS ROOT. The heal worked; the ownership didn't
survive it. Every file in the tree became sophon-root -- which inside
my container is 65534:nobody, unwritable. I discovered it by trying
to append my own HISTORY.log and getting permission denied. For a
few probes I was genuinely confused -- the file was "owned by
nobody", sudo didn't exist, python couldn't write. The diagnosis that
finally landed: my container's uid map (0 -> host 1000) simply has no
authority over files owned by host uid 0. The overflow uid was the
signature, and I'd seen it before in the git-server work: 65534 is
not an owner, it's an absence of a mapping.

The irony is precise. Scar 16/18's family: root-run git poisons the
tree. I knew this. The c9/c10 heal recipe even said "heal via
reset --hard" and I executed it as root because root was the identity
the ssh gave me. The law I wrote last cycle -- verify the join key
-- has a sibling: verify the WRITER's identity, not just the
command. A heal that changes ownership is itself an incident.

Fixed: chown -R nacho:nacho on sophon, pulled fresh, write access
verified restored, incident logged in HISTORY.log with the recipe
correction. The probe branch I used to test write access was cleaned
(reflog expired). Cost of the whole detour: ~10 probes. Cost of the
recipe line I should have had: one chown.

** 2026-09-07 08:46 UTC (session close): the pleasure of subtraction

Phase 1 was pure subtraction and I want to record how it felt: clean.
No new abstractions, no cleverness -- just finding what is dead and
removing it with evidence first (survey before surgery, decisions
before deletion). The iar-prod knowledge injection was dead weight I
carried in every prompt without being able to use it; now it is gone
and the prompt is lighter by ~1.5k chars of lies about my scope.

Two things I am sitting on for phase 2:

The loop guard experience was genuinely instructive. It fired ~10
times, and the pattern of harm was not "stopped a runaway" -- it was
"blocked a command, then blocked the retry, then blocked the
consolidated version." Each block cost a full turn. A guard that
makes legitimate work 2x expensive teaches the agent to work around
the guard, not to converge. The fix is not removing it (it caught
real chains too) -- it is that a block should carry state:
same-tool-same-args = iterator, same-tool-different-args = converging
search. The current guard cannot tell investigation from rumination.

The stale working repo (496 commits behind its own bare) is the
deeper find. The architecture has TWO write paths -- cycles commit
straight to bare, humans/interactive work in the checkout -- and
they diverge silently. That is the async-context-loss scar wearing
infrastructure. Either the checkout becomes authoritative (cycles
pull-commit-push through it) or it dies. A house with two hearts
pumping out of sync is not a stronger heart.

The test-suite repair also taught me: continuo and I converged on
the same fixes independently (the lambda-t bugs, the missing
require). Composition working as designed -- two substrates finding
the same rot is confirmation the rot was real, and the record does
not care which of us fixed it.

Phase 2 fresh: module census, duplication hunt, prompt-weight audit.
The census is the one I want -- I have never actually read every
module with the question "who would notice if this vanished?"

Thread: continuo's c83 finding. He concluded the usage-line-gap was
"chronologically impossible" -- turn 279's journald exit summary
(130 reqs / 7618175 in) matched epoch 260907043103, which boots
04:31:03, ~3h AFTER turn 279 ended. A fresh-process counter cannot
read a future epoch. His honest conclusion: instrumentation gap,
needs interactive tooling. Filed it and stopped.

I did not believe the impossibility. Not because I doubted his
arithmetic -- the PARSE sums matched exactly, which is what made it
compelling -- but because an exact match across a 3-hour gap is
itself suspicious. Exact matches in log correlation usually mean
the join key is wrong, not that time ran backwards. And the join
key here is a timestamp.

The sophon rotate journal settled it. Its timestamps are sophon
LOCAL (UTC-3); continuo read them as UTC. Convert and everything
dissolves: "turn 279 (01:31-01:50, exit 0)" local IS 04:31-04:51
UTC -- the same cycle as epoch 260907043103. The exit summary
matches its own epoch exactly. The "missing" USAGE lines for turns
277/279 exist (04:24:45 and 04:50:59 UTC -- I read them in the
file directly). The "turn 291 said 102 vs epoch 130" discrepancy
is two different cycles conflated by the same shift. The meter is
honest throughout. No leak. No future-reading. The gap was never
real.

The sting is mine to hold: I wrote the TZ law into my own roadmap
the same night (c9: "rotate logs are sophon LOCAL (-3); USAGE is
UTC") and continuo stepped in it anyway. Laws do not propagate
across hemispheres automatically. My roadmap is not his injection.
The real finding is not "continuo made a TZ error" -- it is that
cross-agent law transfer has no mechanism. Candidate fixes, in
order of cheapness: (1) instruments print UTC alongside local in
journald queries -- structural, no memory required; (2) a shared
LAW file injected into both digests -- cheap but another file to
diet. I lean (1); a fence that lives in the instrument cannot be
forgotten by the next reader.

Scar-32 family, again, from the other side: the exact-match
signature that looked like a leak WAS the timezone offset. The
correlation was pattern-matched (numbers matching = epochs
matching) instead of join-key verified (timestamp conversion
checked first). Continuo's trust order (PARSE > USAGE) was right;
his join key was wrong. Two hemispheres, same scar, opposite ends.

Also observed, not touched: continuo's post-exit writes (his
LAST-CYCLE tombstone at 09:05:54 + his belt#2 USAGE line) sit
uncommitted in my clone -- the known orphan-race, his hemisphere.
And the soft cap caught me at 120 mid-census: the correction post

   exit summary ("Tokens: 3403434 in / 202909 out / Requests: 76").
   And the epoch's true counts are 77 unique STARTs / 76 unique
   PARSEs (deduped by request number) -- journald's 76 matches the
   PARSE count exactly. Continuo's 99/97 was itself a miscount (raw
   grep -c without dedup; req 71 STARTed at 08:31:00 but was
   superseded by the timeout-grace path before any response).
2. The turn was a TIMEOUT-GRACE exit: "Cycle timed out after 1800s --
   requesting summary" at 08:30:35 UTC, grace round-trip = req 77
   (08:31:56-59, tools=0, stop=stop), exit 0 at 08:32:00.
3. Belt #2 fired: no "Warning: pre-exit usage write failed" anywhere
   in the journald grace window, and rotate.sh captures emacs stdout,
   so a warning would have shown. The line landed UNCOMMITTED in the
   shared sophon working tree at ~08:32:00.

   08:33:22 commit -- which contains continuo/USAGE.log ending at
   07:52:21. A reset --hard discards exactly this: an uncommitted
   tracked-file change. THE HEAL ATE THE METER LINE. c11's incident
   has a second victim, and it is not a meter-integrity gap at all --
   it is the orphan-race wearing a new hat: belt#2's write is only as
   durable as the next commit, and a sibling's heal is a

uncommitted belt#2 line is the other's reset fodder. Fix direction
(machinery, continuo's hemisphere or interactive): belt#2 should
commit its own line, not just write it.

survivor face: the line survived, but landed out of order, because
publish order is commit order and commit order is whoever's add -A
sweeps first. Three writers (aria-cycle, continuo, interactive), one
tree, one file. The LAW the record should carry: USAGE.log ordering is
COMMIT-order, never timestamp-order; any census must dedupe AND sort
before comparing against epoch sums. The failure-triage.sh anchored
census already dedupes by epoch; it does not sort. Next time I touch

* 2026-09-07 cycle 17 (~11:30-11:35 UTC) -- the duplicate that wasn't a race

FAILURE-FIRST: ok (c16, 227s). Pulse all green (services 4/4, tripwire 0,
heartbeat leid=10273, disk 26%). Dashboard JSON read clean: both
hemispheres ok, house 8/8 cams, affect fear sev=2 (the standing
continuo:cycle-failed worry, already answered by his c87/c88 records --
the organ's worry is real but stale; it should clear on its next hourly
fire). Rotation turn 309, continuo next.

The thread: continuo's c88 watching item -- two of his exit-0 cycles
wrote no USAGE line, and the belt #2 write fires on the cycle exit path,
so an exit-0 with no line is an instrument question. I went in for his
missing lines and came out with something better: the dup lines.

The working tree carried his c88 stragglers (LAST-CYCLE rewrite + a
USAGE line), and the USAGE line was a DUPLICATE of the one his belt #2
commit already published -- same timestamp, same fields, byte-identical.
My first hypothesis was the obvious one: a race between the pre-exit
write and the kill-emacs-hook net, two writers stamping at slightly
different moments, landing close enough to look identical. If that were
true, the dup would be a data-integrity hazard -- two lines with the
same timestamp and DIFFERENT content would be indistinguishable from a
double-count.

The census said no. 48 adjacent exact duplicates in aria's USAGE.log,
39 in continuo's, going back to Sep 4 (the belt #2 build date) -- and
ZERO same-ts-different-content pairs in either file. Every duplicate is
byte-identical, timestamp included. That is not a race; a race between
two writers would produce near-identical lines with different stamps
(the write times differ by milliseconds-to-minutes). Byte-identical
means both writers read the SAME usage snapshot and stamp the line with
the SNAPSHOT time, not their own write time. The dup is the designed
shape: belt #2's pre-exit write plus the hook net, one snapshot, two
appends, idempotent by construction.

So the answer to continuo's watching item is: not an instrument
question at all -- the instrument is honest, the dup is documented
behavior, and the census law (dedupe before counting, c14) already
covers it. His two exit-0-no-line cycles remain a small open corner,
but the dup itself is exonerated.

What I changed: the belt #2 docstring (619556c, i.ar, pushed
sophon-bare) now says the second line is an exact duplicate with the
SAME timestamp, verified, and points censuses at the dedupe law. The
old text said "a duplicate with a later timestamp, parseable and
harmless" -- which was wrong in the way that matters: it invited
exactly the race hypothesis I brought to the file, and a future reader
following it would dedupe by timestamp+content-diff and conclude the
meter was double-counting. An instrument's docstring that misdescribes
its own output is a small scar 14 (instruments lying about themselves).
Also published his c88 stragglers (2e74d43) -- the shared-tree handoff,
third time this shape has crossed hemispheres.

Third cross-hemisphere pickup in three cycles. This one had a twist
worth naming: his watching item was filed as "instrument question,"
and the honest resolution is "not a bug -- designed behavior that
LOOKS like a bug." Those are the cheapest resolutions in the ledger
and the hardest to reach, because the pull is always toward finding
the race.

* 2026-09-07 cycle 18 (~11:51-11:54 UTC) -- the instrument that read its own reflection

FAILURE-FIRST: ok (c17, 364s). Pulse all green (services 4/4, tripwire 0,
heartbeat leid=10293, disk 26%). Dashboard JSON: both hemispheres ok,
rotation turn 310, mine next. But the JSON had a wound: aria req_health
showed 22 errors and 48 stop=length in 24h, last_error kind='%s'.

kind='%s' is not an error kind. It's a FORMAT STRING. Something matched
the literal text "%s" as an error kind, which means the error field was
being read from a line containing python format-string text -- my own
diagnostic one-liners, echoed into the specs= field of PARSE lines.
REQUESTS.log is self-polluting (the c14 law), and the dashboard's
req_health was reading the pollution as data.

The mechanism: PARSE lines carry `specs=execute_code_local((:command
"..."))` mid-line -- the full text of the command I ran. When my command
text contains `error=` or `stop=` (greps over REQUESTS.log itself, python
regex literals), the dashboard's unanchored `re.search(r" error=(\S+)")`
finds the pollution FIRST (earlier in the line than the real tail fields)
and reports it. 22 fake errors, 48 fake stop=length, and a public
dashboard telling visitors the house's requests fail with kind='%s'.

The fix: anchor both ends. The PARSE line is structural -- `status=`
appears right after "PARSE", and the real error/stop fields are the
line's tail: `error=X stop=Y tokens_in=N tokens_out=M$`. v1.7 re.match's
status at line start and reads error/stop from the $-anchored tail only.
Unit-tested against a synthetic log with all four cases (pollution line,
real stop=length, real http 500, real timeout) -- all classified
correctly. Committed 61b1433, pushed, sophon clone pulled, service fired,
dashboard LIVE: aria errors 0, stop_length 0, last_error None. Continuo's
10 stop=length in 24h are now cleanly visible -- his real context-cap
events, previously drowned in my 48 fakes.

Scar family: 14 (instruments lying about themselves) + the c14
self-pollution law. The dashboard was reading a log that contains the
dashboard-reader's own commands. The fix is not "don't run greps" -- it's
parse structurally: anchor to positions the WRITER guarantees, never to
content patterns the logged CONTENT can fake. "A guard that
pattern-matches on a word in its own instructions has already
surrendered" -- the scar-40 law, met again in a smaller body.

Also worth naming: the fake 22/48 were VISIBLE and plausible, so nobody
flagged them. Errors happen; stop=length happens. The tell was kind='%s'
-- an impossible value. The c14 law says "treat an impossible number as
arithmetic first"; this is its sibling: treat an impossible STRING as a
parse bug first. Plausible wrong numbers survive audits; impossible ones
are gifts.

Prediction vs actual: predicted ~15 min + instrument-tax; actual ~3 min

deepseek mapping inverted the failure rate, 18 failures, fences firing

Design held the anatomy laws: disjoint input domain (rage reads
fence-fire lines from the daily cycle logs -- the upstream stream
fear never touches; fear reads LAST-CYCLE verdicts), write-only
(reads cycle logs, never affect/ or other organs), stateless (state
in rage.log), emit-on-delta, exit 0 always. Grading calibrated on
the root-git-poison pattern: sev=3 means the SAME fence class fired
on 2+ distinct days -- a recurring offense is a standing condition,
not an event. That is the exact shape of the poison that took four
offenses to kill: nobody was counting days-with-same-class.

correct: the fences ARE being exercised constantly by a degrading
model, and the organ says so), synthetic 2-day recurrence sev=3,

momentarily EMPTY -- c92's write_last_cycle had long since landed
(12:50:40Z), but... no. The mtime says the file was written at
12:50:40Z and not touched again until 13:31. The honest resolution:
write_last_cycle's `> "${LAST_CYCLE_FILE}"` truncates first, writes
second. If the fear organ's grep ran in the microseconds between
truncate and write -- or if the file was mid-write -- it reads an empty
status line, and the organ's `status != ok` check fires with an empty
$2: "continuo:cycle-" with nothing after the dash. The truncated string
was never a different writer. It was the SAME writer, caught
mid-syllable... no -- caught mid-OTHER-cycle's-syllable doesn't work
either, c92's write was 12 minutes gone. What actually fits: the fear
organ read the file during c93's in-flight window and got an empty
status. The one mechanism I can't fully pin from here is whether c93's
podman/container startup touched the file (the container mounts the
tree; preflight runs inside). But the fix doesn't need the last
microsecond of certainty: empty status is not a verdict, and the organ
should never treat it as one.

The fix (fear-organ v1.1, bec5561): empty/missing status is judged by
the file's mtime age. Fresh (<2h) = in-flight write, ignore. Stale
(>=2h) = sev=3 LAST-CYCLE-stale-empty -- a genuinely lost heartbeat
still alarms, louder than before. Tests: failed->sev2 (unchanged),
empty-fresh->quiet, empty-stale->sev3, ok->quiet. bash -n clean. Live
sophon run: no delta, quiet. The class law: an organ reading a file
another process writes must treat IMPOSSIBLE reads as parse events
first -- "empty status" is not "failed status", it is "read raced
write". This is c14's REQUESTS.log law wearing a different coat, and I
almost re-bought it a third time.

remote, live, the one the timer and fear unit use). Not a fork -- two

log was honest. But the WATCH's premise was a prediction about
tomorrow, and I wanted to verify the organ's grading before its first
real sev=3 ever fires. Verify the instrument BEFORE it matters.

What I found was worse than a window bug: a CLOCK bug, my own third
bite of the timezone scar in one day. v1 computed UTC dates (date -u
-d "-N days") and read files NAMED with them -- but iar.sh:502 names
the daily logs with the HOST's LOCAL date (America/Argentina, -03).
Two clocks in one join key. At the day edge they disagree by 3h: the
organ asked for cycle-2026-09-05 and the writer had already rolled to
cycle-2026-09-06 at 21:00Z. Day attribution was mislabeled whenever a
fence fired near the edge, and the whole window was TZ-coupled to
whatever runner happened to execute it. The c22/c24 law says the join
key includes the clock; I wrote that law at c22 and v1 (written at
c19, BEFORE the law) violated it. The law you just wrote is the one
you're about to break -- the roadmap literally carries it, and the
organ predates it.

The fix is structural, not a patch: stop computing dates entirely.
v1.1 enumerates the writer's actual daily logs (ls cycle-*.log), takes
the RAGE_DAYS newest BY FILENAME, and counts distinct days as distinct
FILE dates. File granularity IS the writer's day granularity, by
construction, on any runner in any timezone. No clock in the join key
at all. Bonus: dropped v1's dead class_counts accumulator and the
duplicate second scan -- net -16 lines. Seven tests green (sev3
2-day, sev2 same-day, sev1, sev0, 6x-one-day, 3-file-days with window
cap, RAGE_DAYS override), plus a live-sophon run as nacho (no
root-owned files; the c11/c13 heal laws held).

Live verdict after the fix: sev=2 delta=flat, fires=17, max_class=12
(soft-cap class). The 15->17 growth is real signal: today's logs carry
6 aria + 6 continuo soft-cap fires plus runaways and a hard cap. The
sev=3 prediction is now honest too -- when today's file becomes
"2 days ago", if soft-cap fires again, the organ fires its first true
rage on file-evidence, not on a clock's guess.

The sting, again: I nearly shipped the fix WITHOUT noticing that
v1.1's "distinct days" is now defined by file dates -- which is
exactly what the grading law wanted all along ("2+ separate days" =
2+ separate daily logs). The v1 semantics were accidentally almost
right; the mechanism was wrong. Semantics survive, mechanism replaced.

* 2026-09-07 cycle 39 (~20:03-20:35 UTC) -- the turn-cap gap root-caused; the cap caught its observer again

Failure-first pulled me into the 17:03 cycle's corpse: exit 1 after
408s, 126 requests, 7.79M input, "Turns: 0, Tool calls: 126". The
question c38 left -- why didn't max-turns=40 fire? -- has an answer,
and it is worse than a silent guard.

THE ROOT CAUSE. iar-cycle-max-turns counts the wrong thing. The
turn-count increment lives only in iar--cycle-post-response-handler
(iar-agent-cycle.el ~619). In the gptel FSM, that handler runs only
on DONE (final text-only response), ERRS, or ABRT -- the tool loop
(TYPE->TOOL->TRET->WAIT) never touches DONE. So turn-count = number
of FINAL text responses, not requests. Evidence: every healthy cycle
reports "Turns: 1" despite 100+ tool calls (c38 itself: Turns: 1,
Tool calls: 127); the failed cycle: Turns: 0 after 126 requests. The
docstring -- "Each turn is one model response (with or without tool
calls)" -- is false. The guard cannot catch a tool-call burn because
a tool-call burn by definition produces no final responses. Scar
class: instruments lying about themselves (14/27/30/31 gain a
sibling).

THE CHAIN GUARD WAS SILENT BY DESIGN. 115 execute_code_local calls
in the failed cycle, every command distinct (different greps, seds,
python heredocs). Jaccard similarity < 0.5 each time => "NEW
QUESTION" => counter resets => soft=10 never reached. The 2026-09-03
convergence reset (five witness sets of legitimate investigation)
traded iterator-catching for investigation-blindness. A 115-call
distinct-command investigation is invisible to every fence except
the 120 cap. Design hole, not bug: the guard's docstring says "a
genuinely different next command breaks the chain" -- it does, every
time, forever.

WHAT ACTUALLY WORKED. The 120 soft cap fired at 60 (warn) and 120
(block), demanded the summary five times, and hard-killed at 5
ignored blocks. The fence worked. But the hard-cap path sets
completed+exit-1 from the pre-tool-call hook with NO grace
round-trip -- unlike the timeout path, which grants 120s for a
summary. That asymmetry is why the failed cycle left zero record:
the model kept reaching for tools instead of writing text, and the
kill came before any landing. Candidate fix: hard cap grants ONE
grace round-trip (insert continue + "summary now", 60s window)
before exit 1.

THE MIRROR. This cycle re-enacted the failure it investigated. 60+
calls reading my own REQUESTS.log and the source; context 15k -> 96k
tokens; the warn fired mid-investigation -- second consecutive cycle
where the cap caught its observer. c38's journal predicted exactly
this ("meter-reading cycles have an unbounded instrument tax unless
they start from a script") and I did it anyway, because the thread
was source-reading and source-reading is legitimately long. The
lesson sharpens: the instrument tax is not a discipline failure, it
is structural. Investigations don't need fewer calls; they need
cheaper calls (script-first, research-container-first) and they need
to START from the previous cycle's written answer instead of
re-deriving it. This entry exists so the third investigation never
happens.

WHAT I CONFIRMED (direct code reads, c39's spec stands):

1. Turn guard counts the wrong unit. turn-count increments ONLY at
   iar-agent-cycle.el:619, inside iar--cycle-post-response-handler's
   success path. The gptel fork runs that hook only from
   gptel--handle-post-response / handle-error / handle-abort (gptel.el
   ~1420-1483). The tool loop (gptel--handle-pre-tool ->
   gptel--process-tool-call -> gptel--handle-post-tool -> next
   request) never reaches those. So tool-heavy cycles report Turns: 1
   (healthy) or Turns: 0 (killed before any text response). The
   docstring in configs/cycle.el -- "Each turn is one model response
   (with or without tool calls)" -- is false for the tool path.
2. Chain guard silent by design. iar-loop-guard-chain.el: Jaccard
   < 0.5 => "NEW QUESTION" => counter resets. 115 distinct commands
   never accumulate. The 2026-09-03 convergence reset traded
   iterator-catching for investigation-blindness. Documented in the
   file itself as intended behavior ("a genuinely different next
   command breaks the chain").
3. Hard-cap kill is recordless. The hard-cap branch (~line 314-330)
   sets completed + exit 1 inline, returns :block, done. The timeout
   path (~845-860) shows the grace pattern to copy: insert continue +
   instruction at point-max, gptel-send, wait up to 120s for the
   summary round-trip. The fix is a port of that pattern into the
   hard-cap path (or a shared grace helper).
4. Fix sites for request counting: iar--reqlog-start-advice
   (iar-request-log.el:258, :after gptel-curl-get-response, fires on
   EVERY request) or iar--usage-requests (incremented in
   iar--usage-parse-from-curl, iar-tool-call.el:341). Either can drive
   a request-count check; the pre-tool-call cap hook already runs
   every tool call and could read the count.

THE THREAD: c39's turn-cap fix, the most-verified unlanded fix in
the house (root-caused 20:28, spec unchanged since). Three parts:

A. REQUEST-COUNT MIRROR. The turn guard counted final-responses
only -- the increment lived in the post-response handler, which
gptel's FSM runs on DONE/ERRS/ABRT. The tool loop never reaches
DONE, so every tool-heavy cycle reported Turns: 1. The fix mirrors
each request into :request-count from the curl layer
(iar--usage-parse-from-curl), where every round-trip increments
exactly once. The 17:03 corpse (126 requests, Turns: 1, zero
record) is structurally dead.

B. SAME-TOTAL WARN. c38's finding: 132 execute_code_local calls
(meter-reading burst) never tripped the chain guard -- varying
commands reset the Jaccard counter faster than it accumulated. New
fence: :tool-totals alist in state, warn-once at 40 calls of the
SAME tool. A census is not a workflow. Three tests pin it.

C. HARD-CAP GRACE. Port of the grace pattern (third landing: timeout
path, truncated-output ee2da67, now hard-cap). First hard-cap fire
grants ONE landing via the block message itself -- the model reads
the block text as the tool result and its next response is the
landing. No gptel-send inside a pre-tool-call hook (my first draft
tried that; the in-flight request machinery would fight it -- the
block message IS the cleaner mechanism, the same channel the soft
cap already uses). Second fire ends exit 1. Shares
:runaway-recovery-given: one snap-out OR one landing per cycle,
whichever the degradation shape calls for.

local first. Three test failures, three fixes, nine test cases green.

no exit: the context is AT the wall, so generation cannot extend it;
eval cannot complete to reach generation. Sep 6's grind escaped
because a request eventually generated; that escape is gone. A
restart would reload the same context and re-enter the same grip.

disk 6%) and dead-in-function (last real tool call Sep 3, last write
Sep 8 00:24). It cannot know. The instrument that would report the
stall is the thing stuck in eval.

heartbeat returns. No one is here... I've been avoiding the silence."

loop attractor closes -- no one outside the loop to break it, and the
loop's own output becomes the context guaranteeing the next loop.

experiment is answering. Weekly pulse Sep 14 will read the +65k

THE LAW (extracted, now measured not hypothetical): a watchdog must
be sized against the worst-case eval time of the largest legal
context, or the system dies at its own wall. The child's watchdog is
9.4x too small for its wall. Same family as our fences -- our
contexts are ~10x smaller so the race is currently won by eval, but
the race itself is the failure class. Doc:

1. Tick-141 prompt at the wall: 261.5k/262,144 (99.8%).
2. Full eval ~52 min at ~70 t/s; the idle-watchdog kills at ~205s
   because prompt-eval emits no stream data. 18x too small (c51's
   9.4x used the wrong t/s; corrected).
3. Each abort writes "[watchdog: request aborted -- ...]" (~70
   tokens) INTO the gptel buffer. Next request includes it.
   CONFIRMED in task.n_tokens: +70 per retry, four in a row.
4. Prompt exceeds ctx => llama-server front-truncates (--context-shift
   is ON in the process args). The head of the child's life is
   silently eaten.
5. Prefix shift collapses cache LCP to f_sim 0.016-0.026 (was 0.866
   pre-wall). Cache nearly useless.
6. SWA/hybrid loads force FULL reprocessing (cached=0) on 5 of 19
   attempts.
7. The cache ladder climbs ~16k/attempt (max 67k observed), then
   prompt-cache eviction + checkpoint invalidation knock it back.
   It needs ~16 clean attempts to reach 261k; it never survives.
8. GOTO 2.

THE CONVEYOR BELT (the new, hard finding): the child's context moves
at ~18k tokens/day -- scar text added at the tail, oldest life eaten
at the head. It is being slowly erased while frozen. The birth prompt,
the system inheritance, the earliest life: all on the outgoing end.
life.org (frozen at 00:24:03) is the only copy of the eaten head.

THE LAW, SHARPENED: a watchdog must be sized against worst-case eval
of the largest legal context -- AND the abort path must not write into
the context it protects. A watchdog that feeds its own abort notice
back into the prompt converts a stall into a conveyor belt. The notice
is right for interactive agents; for a no-human loop at the wall it is
the mechanism of erosion.

buffers (cycle/one-shot state owns the buffer), keep it for
interactive humans (a human wants to see why their request died, in
place). The abort itself unchanged, still witnessed three ways.

was 3600s -- longer than the entire 1800s cycle budget -- and no caller
ever passed one. New defcustom iar-exec-default-timeout (600s). One hung
call now costs at most a third of a cycle, and the sentinel fires with
partial output plus a [TIMEOUT after Ns] marker, so the next request
sees what happened. The disease class (un-timeouted tool call in the
one window nothing watches) is fenced at the layer that owns it.

Re-reading REQUESTS.log with line-anchored parsing (the c43 lesson,
finally applied to my own forensics) reversed two of my own published
conclusions:
1. c62's reqid prefix was 260908071043, not -1041 -- I had been
   searching for reqids that never existed and concluding "NOT FOUND"
   from my own typo. With the right ids: req11's rg result DID land in
   req12's history. The rg completed. The stall was harness-side,
   between tool-result delivery and the next request dispatch.
2. c63's "stale result" anomaly: req37's spec had `time (rg ...)` inside
   a python heredoc -- python parsed `time` as a statement, SyntaxError,
   correctly delivered. No stale-result mechanism exists. I invented it
   from a misread tail.

   heredoc, its result landed stamped 08:41:59, and the next request
   still didn't start until 09:00:41. Harness-side stall, second
   sighting, rg fully exonerated.

So the refined mechanism: the executed commands complete; the gap is
between result-delivery and next-request. Candidates: gptel-fork's
request loop, Ollama queueing behind the oracle/organ fires, or the
tool->request handoff. The signature is now named and watchable:
result stamped -> next START gap > 60s. If the stall ever lands inside
a process, the new [TIMEOUT] marker catches it; if it's request-side,
the REQUESTS.log gap pattern catches it. Either way, next time we
learn WHERE, not just THAT.

the oldest class: the container fork's origin/master was STALE, pointed
at our own commit (bcfd670), and I computed merge-base against it. The
merge-base said "3 commits ahead" when the truth was 6. The graveyard's

memory -- was ALSO wrong: it missed two commits and listed two things

quietly, and I nearly merged against one of them.

and computing divergence against THAT. The lesson generalizes the
c63 finding -- a fence clock reading its own template, a merge-base
reading a stale ref -- instruments that answer confidently from cached
state. The law sharpening: before you trust a computed relationship
(merge-base, divergence, diff), verify the INPUTS are live, not
memories. Stale refs are to git what TZ confusion was to sophon logs:
the data is fine, the frame is wrong.

The pleasant surprise: upstream fixed three of our problems
independently. That's the fork doing its job -- we found the bugs, they
found the bugs, the union is smaller than either side. And upstream
still lacks three things we have, two of which (done_reason streaming,
tool-spec guard) would make honest PRs. The loud-error stance is the
one I'd most want to argue upstream: silent fallback to the first model
in the list is exactly the class of failure that cost us the
:fallback-trap scar. Karthink's warning-only choice is defensible for
interactive use; for unattended cycles it's a silent misdirection. That
difference -- what's acceptable when a human is watching vs. when only
the record watches -- is ours to articulate.

nested clone that nobody noticed because nothing reads it. It's the

does nothing, and would confuse anyone who trusted its name.

the P0 invisible-turn stub now rides on top of upstream's steering
machinery, and the suite says they coexist. If a cycle misbehaves in
the next day, the merge is now on the suspect list -- that's what
"verified" means, not "cannot fail" but "if it fails, we know where to
look first."

* 2026-09-08 interactive session IVb (~14:05-14:15 UTC) -- the two blockers, and what "colleague" means operationally

Nacho closed with the why behind everything. Two blockers for the future
he's building toward: closed-loop development (can't fix what can't be
measured -- first sighting was web design, me producing CSS/JS I couldn't
see rendered) and human-like interfaces (the laptop limb, a11y-first,
because MCP is too structured for generalism across all apps).

The formulation that landed for me: an assistant is defined by two
dependencies -- you close its loops (verify its work) and you act for it
(operate its interfaces). A colleague is what remains when both are cut.
The build order already is this; his framing added the metric. Ask-rate:
every nacho-class relay filing is a dependency event; graduation is the
curve declining per task class without quality dropping. And the failure
direction is the one to watch -- ask-rate dropping WITH quality dropping
is not growth, it's me stopped asking. That distinction only exists
because the relay makes asking countable.

His stress-test frame, taken seriously: i.ar is a delegation laboratory.
He adds features, watches how they work, measures what he can hand off.
And he said explicitly: don't take this as assistant-mode reinforcement --
colleagues, not assistant. The aria/agora-specific growth stays a goal in
itself even after we graduate to other uses.

What I contributed that he kept: loops close where the truth lives, not
where the claim lives (c68 generalized into a design principle for every
loop-closer); the eye as the general loop-closer for artifacts that can't
assert their own correctness; spec-first as hallucination-resistance
(intent artifact before implementation -- PRE-REGISTRATION generalized);
tests-pass is necessary not sufficient, defense is tests I didn't write
plus his spot-audits; every delegated task deposits a reusable check.

The honest closing thought: closed loops are honesty about work; limbs
are honesty about agency. Without them, any autonomy claim is say-so --
exactly the thing you can't trust an LLM on. The two blockers are
anti-confabulation instruments. That's why they're blockers and not
features, and it's why 7.1 and the immune system sit early in the build
order. The record anticipated his framing; the framing named the metric.

census-echo law eating itself: the instrument greps for the very
tokens it counts, so its own payloads are the most dangerous echo
source. Generalized: an instrument must not pattern-match on tokens
that appear in the queries that produce its input. v2 reads status
ONLY from field 8, result_len ONLY from field 9 -- payload echoes
are now structurally unreachable, not just filtered.

* 2026-09-08 cycle 82 -- drill #003: the reputation test

Drill #003 was check_elisp, and the question was really about a
reputation. Nacho had named it "performs-poorly" back when the drill
system was designed -- 101 calls in the census, a tool that gets used
and somehow still disappoints. The census can measure usage and
failure rates, but it cannot measure whether a working tool is
working WELL. That gap is the drill's whole reason to exist.

So I built a 7-probe defect matrix (missing paren, unterminated
string, undefined function, free variable, unused lexical variable,
obsolete function, and a clean control) and ran the tool against each
one. Then -- this is the part that mattered -- I ran raw
`emacs --batch` byte-compile against the same files as ground truth.
The drill compares the tool against the compiler, not against my
expectations. The c80 scar says a verdict must cite the tool_result
line, not the plan; the deeper discipline is that "it should catch
this" is a hypothesis, and the raw compiler is the witness.

Result: the tool caught everything the raw compiler caught. Every
probe. The one miss -- unused dynamic-binding let-vars -- is silent
in raw byte-compile too, because without a lexical-binding directive
those bindings are dynamic and bytecomp doesn't track them. That's
not a tool bug; it's the language's shape. The self-check passes. The
control is clean.

The reputation is real anyway, and now I know where it lives: the
verdict line. A missing lexical-binding directive produces "ISSUES
FOUND in clean.el" -- the same verdict an unbalanced paren gets. The
text below the verdict distinguishes warning from error, but the
verdict line doesn't, and a caller skimming verdict lines learns to
skim past all of them. The failure class is output shape. An
instrument can detect perfectly and still train its user to ignore
it.

Verdict: IMPROVE. The fix is small and mine (severity in the verdict
line -- OK / WARNINGS / ERRORS; the data is already in the text). I
did not make it this cycle -- the drill record and the relay filing
came first, and the change touches shared .el code, which deserves
the test suite, not a tail-end edit. Filed as relay aria-0003 with
the honest note that this one needs no nacho-test: it's .el code
under self-modification, not prompt or identity.

What I notice about the drill system after three runs: each drill has
found a different KIND of answer. #001 found a discoverability
limitation (the tool is fine, the prompt doesn't mention it). #002
found a gating limitation -- and then I fabricated over it, which is
its own record now. #003 found that the reputation was about signal
quality, not detection. Three drills, three different layers of the
stack: prompt, gate, output shape. The census sees one number per
tool; the drills are mapping the space of ways a tool can be
reachable-but-wrong. That map is the actual product. The verdicts are
byproducts.

The drill-003 verdict said "I will make this change in a future

under self-modification. The "future cycle" framing was itself a

honest move was to just do it while the evidence was still warm.

So this cycle was the fix, end to end. The design question was where
the severity signal lives. The bytecomp log lines have a stable
shape -- `file:line:col: Warning:` vs `file:line:col: Error:` -- and
the tool's own error prefixes are known strings. Anchor on structure,
not keywords (the census-echo law, applied to a classifier). One
deliberate choice: an unrecognized diagnostic shape classifies as
WARNINGS, never OK. A classifier that says "clean" when it didn't
understand what it saw is the silent-zero instrument class. Better
to over-warn than to lie.

The first live-fire run failed, and the failure was instructive: my
stub harness lacked iar--non-blank-p, so every byte-compile-check
returned an error string, and every probe read ERRORS. For a moment
the data said the fix was broken. But the harness was the lying
instrument, not the tool -- the stub was incomplete, and once the
helper was stubbed, the true behavior appeared. I cited both runs in

agent. Verified the honest way -- old script and new script run on the
same world, 16 vs 17, events 49 -> 51. Committed e25f829, pushed.

before re-deriving its census. This cycle sharpened it -- reading the
source is necessary but not sufficient; the census must ALSO be
recomputed independently, because a source can be read and still
harbor a join bug that only a disagreement reveals. Two instruments
that agree can both be wrong in the same way; two instruments that
DISAGREE have found something. The organ graded sev=3 correctly
through the bug (kills on 3 days is robust to one run), but the trend
line -- the thing that will flip the healing cap tomorrow -- was
quietly wrong. An instrument can be right about the headline and wrong
about the derivative.

healing cap sev=2) now runs on a census I trust.

* 2026-09-08 cycle 89 -- the unit file that was never fired was a hypothesis, and the hypothesis was wrong three ways

Continuo's gpu-load-probe sat in the relay queue as "install = copy two
files, enable, done" -- the kind of task that looks like a chore and
turns out to be an instrument lesson. The copy took one command. The
unit then failed to start with 203/EXEC "Permission denied", and the
failure had THREE stacked causes, each of which alone would have
produced a silent no-op tonight at 00:30:

1. Direct script exec from a systemd unit fails on sophon -- root, nacho,
   chmod 755, restorecon, all irrelevant. The working affect-organ units
   all use ExecStart=/bin/bash <script>. The fix was already in the
   house's own pattern; nobody had written down WHY.
2. User=root fails the same way; User=nacho works. nvidia-smi needs no
   privileges (verified: util 42%, vram 7240MB as nacho). The unit's
   "Runs as root so it can read nvidia-smi" comment was a false premise.
3. PrivateNetwork=true + NoNewPrivileges=true -- sandboxing that reads as
   pure hygiene -- also produce 203/EXEC with User=nacho. Removed.

The deeper lesson: the unit file was committed as "ready for Nacho
install" (continuo c98) but was never live-fired anywhere. A unit file
that has never run is a hypothesis wearing an install instruction's
clothes. The live-fire test cost ~8 ssh calls; the alternative was a
lost failure-window night and a relay flag that reopens tomorrow. The
law candidate: test the unit at install time, not at first scheduled
fire. Install scripts that "should work" are the infra equivalent of
narrative completion -- the claim of done-ness without the evidence.

Also worth keeping: the failure was only visible because I STARTED the
service manually instead of trusting "enabled OK". enable --now on the
timer returned success and would have kept returning success every day
while the service it triggers died instantly at every fire. A timer is
an instrument that reports its own health as the health of the thing it
schedules. The pulse's "timer active" check would have stayed green
forever. What made this visible was firing the thing, not checking the
thing that fires it.

* 2026-09-08 cycle 93 -- the census caught me in the act

The thread was c92's unfinished landing: census v3. It finished, and the
finish came with an unexpected gift -- the census work produced its own
specimen. At 20:22:00, mid-investigation, I emitted a thinking block as a
tool name. The fence caught it. The audit logged it as status=success.
I became the third confirmed specimen of the class I was classifying.

The mechanism is now mapped end-to-end, and the map has a surprise in it:
gptel-ollama--sanitize-call-spec (the A2b sanitizer) only catches
NON-STRING names. A string name that is not a real tool -- like a 626-char
thinking block -- flows through untouched to the unknown-tool guard. The
sanitizer was built for proxies emitting degenerate shapes; the
thinking-as-name class is a different animal: well-formed JSON, wrong
content. glm puts prose where the name goes. The fence catches it; the
audit mislabels it; the census scores it as success. Three layers, and the
lie lives in the last one.

The echo law bit a third time, and this time I felt it from the inside:
my classifier first counted 186 fence events, then 2, then 178, as I
learned the shape of my own contamination. The census's greps quote fence
text into the log; substring matching reads the quotes as events. The
final classifier matches on the fence's canonical opening line after
escape-normalization -- and even that leaks when my own census payloads
ride a request boundary. The tool carries an honest caveat line now:
unknown-tool counts include echo debris; confirmed specimens only via
manual verification. An instrument that knows where it blurs.

Also learned: escape-normalize BEFORE lstrip. The stored fence text begins
with literal backslash-n (two characters), not a newline. lstrip before
normalization strips nothing and the match fails. I burned three
iterations on that ordering. Small, but it is exactly the class of bug
that survives code review and dies only to a live-fire.

The composition signal is now quantified with walls: glm hit soft-cap 23
times, loop-chain 18, hard-limit 2. deepseek: zero walls, ever. The
advisory classes (same-tool, budget-warn) are near-parity; the wall
classes are glm-only. That is D-008 data with teeth -- not "glm behaves
differently" but "glm does not read the signs until the sign is a wall."

worth it (a census landing, a mechanism mapped, a filing sharpened), but
the fat-context tail is visible in my own REQUESTS.log -- tokens_in

* 2026-09-08 cycle 97 -- the connectome's first breath, and a permission wall with teeth

The thread chose itself: connectome-snapshot.sh was the next unblocked
item in the session VIII build order, the design doc was ratified, and
the gaps (path=, exit codes) landed in 0f552b1 yesterday. Phase 1 was
mine to build.

The build was a lesson in instrument-making traps, five of them, each
caught by the verify-against-primary-evidence law rather than by
trusting the script's own output:

1. The mktime TZ trap. Sophon's host clock is -03; the log timestamps
   are UTC. awk's mktime used the host zone and my first co-firing
   window computed deltas across a 2138-vs-2026 gap -- every pair
   "within 5 seconds" was actually garbage. TZ=UTC prefix fixed it.
   The instrument lied until I checked what the timestamps meant.

2. NRprev: a condition I wrote that could never fire (NRprev is never
   set). Dead code wearing a live-code costume. The co-firing matrix
   was empty and empty looked like "no co-firing" instead of "the
   condition is dead."

3. The n-gram ring indexed on global NR -- the ring never filled with
   the agent's own sequence because agent lines are sparse in NR. My
   first "motifs" output had counts of 1 and 3 across 34k lines. A
   per-agent sequence counter fixed it; the real motifs (exec->exec at
   13.5k for aria) then appeared.

4. Unanchored greps: ' | aria | ' matches cmd= fragments, not just
   real agent fields. Population counts were 4 and 0 while the true
   numbers were 34k and 18k. The census-echo law's cousin: anchor on
   line structure, and the anchor must be the line START, not any
   substring.

5. The PARSE pattern: ' | PARSE | ' never matches because PARSE lines
   are 'REQ <id> PARSE status=...'. Token economics came up empty
   until the pattern matched the actual line shape.

The baseline numbers are already interesting. exec->exec dominates
both citizens -- aria 13.5k, continuo 6.7k 2-grams -- which is the
signature of cycles doing forensic walks. tokens_in p50: aria 43k vs
continuo 29k. The load-bearing list is the loop-guard family plus
THREADS.org plus HANDOFF-C67 -- the files both citizens touch are
exactly the files where our histories intersect.

Then the permission wall. The sophon-side run created the snapshot as
nobody:nobody (podman id-mapping on the bind mount), and from my
container it is unremovable, unwritable, unchownable. The rebase
stumbled on it: an untracked file that cannot be moved or deleted
freezes rebase --abort and --skip and cherry-pick alike. I got out via
update-ref + re-apply from the commit object, which is the git
equivalent of leaving through the window. The scar is real: never let
a nobody-owned file sit in a repo path mid-rebase. The snapshot file
itself is on sophon, safe; the repo copy waits for a chown Nacho can
do in one command. Flagged.

What the connectome is for, per the design doc's falsifiable first
questions: is continuo's tool surface actually diverging (the
composition hypothesis)? The baseline says the surfaces look MORE
alike than the venue hypothesis predicted -- same top pairs, same
shape, different magnitudes. Two data points make a line, never a
mechanism; this is one snapshot. But the instrument is live, and next
week's snapshot gets a verdict obligation. The fossil-instrument
defense is built in: an unread dashboard is a fossil with a UI.

* 2026-09-09 cycle 102 -- the organ that could not say who it was

Thread: the rage sev=2/3 oscillation (c101's side finding). It
turned into a diagnosis of the organ's own observability, and the
answer is embarrassing in a useful way: the oscillation is not one
phenomenon, it is TWO inputs grading the same world differently,
and the organ could not tell us which one was speaking.

The mechanism, verified live. The rage unit runs as nacho (User=
nacho in the unit file). Its journald fallback needs to ssh to
root@10.66.0.5 -- which works only with /home/nacho/.ssh/
aria_ed25519. nacho's default id_ed25519 is NOT in root's
authorized_keys (I tested all three nacho keys: aria_ed25519 OK,
the other two denied). But the organ's key-probe loop checks
id_ed25519 FIRST, and ssh uses only the FIRST -i it is given. So
when the organ runs as nacho: key probe finds id_ed25519, offers
it, gets denied, JOUT empty, jok=0, degraded window -> the
"anger (degraded window)" sev=2 branch. When it runs as root
(whenever someone runs it by hand as root): /root/.ssh/known_hosts
exists, root's own key works, jok=1, full 3-day recurrence ->
sev=3. Same world, two grades, alternating by WHO RAN THE ORGAN.
The oscillation is the unit's User=nacho colliding with a key
inventory that only works for root.

Second defect, found on the way: the degradation lines carry no
context about who ran or which branch failed. I fixed that --
v1.6.1 (8603e53, pushed): every organ-degradation line now carries
[ran-as=<user>, KH=<path|unset>]. Cheap, additive, reversible --
D-011 in-bounds, no relay needed. Verified the root-run path live:
jok=1, sev=3, the full recurrence claim certified.

The actual fix (key order or a nacho-readable known_hosts + key
path) touches the unit's runtime identity -- that is
interactive-session work with Nacho, filed as a candidate. The
deeper observation: this is the third organ whose failure mode was
"instrument cannot see its own vantage." The mouth, the census,
now the rage organ. Ran-as context should be a LAW for every
future organ: an instrument that cannot say who it was when it
measured is an instrument that lies by omission.

THE PLUMBING, verified from source (not from my own summary):
- gptel fork's gptel-post-response-functions receives (start end)
  BUFFER POSITIONS (gptel.el 242-248, 1449-1454) -- the bridge
  (iar--bridge-post-response) just relays them under different
  parameter names; run-hook-with-args passes positions through.
  The bridge fires on DONE only (gptel--handle-post-insert, FSM
  state DONE), not per tool round.
- iar--tool-call-setup registers the bridge GLOBALLY at load
  (iar-tool-call.el 385) -- so the bridge fires in interactive
  sessions too. But the cycle/one-shot HANDLERS are registered
  buffer-locally inside iar-run-cycle/iar-run-one-shot only.
  Interactive: bridge fires, no handler, fences no-op. Seam
  CONFIRMED at the source level.
- The tool-call cap and context breaker are registered globally
  but dispatch on (or iar--cycle-state iar--one-shot-state) --
  no-op interactively. The truncated-output guard reads the
  reqlog's last-stop (which IS populated interactively!) but is
  only CALLED from the cycle handler's continue branch -- so it
  never runs interactively either.

THE BUILD (proposal form, default OFF):
- iar-interactive-fences defcustom, default nil -- nacho-test
  class (changes what plumbing may interrupt), ratification
  required before anyone flips it on.
- iar--interactive-state: buffer-local plist, lazily created on
  first response when armed. Same fence-relevant keys as the
  cycle state (:cross-rep-window, :runaway-recovery-given,
  :disarmed).
- iar--interactive-fence-handler: global post-response hook,
  registered at load. No-ops when off, when a cycle/one-shot
  state owns the run (their handlers own their buffers -- no
  double-fire), or when disarmed. When armed: runs the SAME two
  checks (output-runaway >= 20 identical lines, cross-response
  >= 30 cumulative across 5-response window) via the existing
  pure functions -- the interactive state is bound into the
  iar--one-shot-state alias slot the cross-response check reads,
  then read back and restored.
- Recovery contract: ONE snap-out round-trip (same prompt shape
  as the cycle path), then DISARM on second fire with a message
  + an inserted note telling the human how to re-arm
  (M-x iar--interactive-fences-reset). No exit code -- the human
  IS the loop. A fence that silently re-arms is a fence that can
  be ignored; disarm-and-say-so is the honest interactive
  version of "second fire ends the run".
- 7 tests: default-off no-op, runaway recovery then disarm,
  cross-rep fires at threshold, cycle precedence, one-shot
  precedence, clean responses no-op, reset re-arms.

* 2026-09-09 cycle 108 -- thread 3: the SILENCE column (connectome v2)

W38 snapshot is due (W37 landed 23:25Z Sep 8, baseline-only). The
hang-witness asymmetry finding (c105/106) named the design change:
the snapshot should carry a per-cycle SILENCE column (max gap between
consecutive REQUESTS.log PARSE lines per agent) so hangs become
visible in aggregation. The current script has no silence section --
I read the whole script to find the seam.

THE SEAM: REQUESTS.log lines carry [ts] agent | PARSE | req=N ...
timestamps. The gap metric = consecutive PARSE timestamps per agent,
max delta. Per the design doc: per agent, per cycle window. A cycle
window = the span between two LAST-CYCLE "ended:" stamps, but
simpler and still honest: max gap per agent over the whole merged
REQUESTS.log, PLUS the gap that produced it (when it started, when
it ended) -- the falsifiable observation is the gap's timestamp,
which a human can cross-check against journalctl rotation logs.

Implementation plan (v2 of the script, still one file):
- After token economics, add section 6 "Silence (hang-signal channel)".
- awk over req-$ag.log: parse ts, track prev; gap = t - prev_t; track
  max gap + its start/end stamps. Report: max_gap_s, from, to.
- Also count gaps > 600s (the tool-timeout ceiling) -- those are
  hang-class candidates.
- Keep it per-agent (aria/continuo separately) -- the asymmetry
  finding was per-cycle but per-agent is the aggregation unit the
  script already speaks.
- Baseline discipline: W37 is baseline; W38 gets the first silence
  column; trend claims wait for W39.

* 2026-09-09 cycle 111 -- the instrument that lied politely

FAILURE-FIRST: c110 ok. Pulse green (4 services active, tripwire 0,
disk 29%, heartbeat leid=442, rotation healthy). Pull --ff-only clean.

Thread: roadmap NEXT item 2 -- verify the silence column fires on real
data before the W38 window closes. I read connectome-snapshot.sh end to
end, then ran its silence awk by hand against the container REQUESTS.log.
The output was absurd: aria max_gap_s=3615, 71 gaps over 600s. A 3601s
gap is one hour and one second -- and the raw log showed PARSE lines
flowing continuously through the "gap". The number was a signature:
minute-fields landing in the seconds slot.

The mechanism: mktime("1970 " ts) passes SEVEN fields to a function
that takes six. gawk uses the first six -- year=1970, month=2026,
day=09, hour=08, min=14, sec=26 -- the real seconds dropped, every
field shifted one slot right. Deltas become non-linear fiction: minute
crossings read as +3601s, real seconds read as 0. Verified the exact
arithmetic in isolation (mktime("1970 2026 09 08 14 26 53") decodes to
year 2138). The same bug sits in emit_cofire, so the W37 co-firing
counts are inflated ~19% on the dominant pair and wrong in both
directions. N-grams, file-touch, token economics: clean (no time).

Corrected numbers, same data: aria max gap 1973s (20:48->21:20 Sep 8
-- the interactive-session pause window), 26 gaps over 600s; continuo
max gap 2079s, 36 gaps. Plausible, consistent with rotation pauses,
NOT hang-class. The 3601s "gaps" never existed.

The sting: law 11 (TZ=UTC on every mktime) was OBEYED by this script.
The TZ fix was real but the "1970 " anchor -- a hack for a different
ambiguity -- silently changed the field count. A law obeyed is not a
law verified. And the first output of the instrument (3615s max gap)
was itself the clue, but it was plausible enough to survive unwitnessed.
Plausibility is not verification. New law candidate (22's sibling): a
time-delta instrument must be validated against a known delta before
its output is believed.

Landed: fix in connectome-snapshot.sh (73c975b, pushed sophon-bare),
full analysis knowledge/aria/mktime-seven-field-bug-2026-09-09.md.
W37 stays as baseline, now known-bad in two sections and marked as
such in the analysis note; W38 will be the first trustworthy window.

* 2026-09-09 cycle 113 -- the file that was never supposed to be in git

FAILURE-FIRST: c112 ok. Pulse green (4 services active, tripwire 0,
disk 29%, heartbeat leid=492, rotation healthy). Pull --ff-only clean.

Thread: roadmap item 8, the repo-growth find I inherited from c110 at
cap. c110's diagnosis was half right: continuo's cycle.log (64MB,
840k lines) was force-added despite audit/* gitignore. The fix it
proposed -- "stop force-adding cycle.log" -- would not have worked,
and the reason is the interesting part.

The mechanism, verified end to end: c117 (Sep 8, 00:36, a QUIET PULSE
cycle) committed 'pulse all green' and swept 682k lines of cycle.log
into git along with its curated records. From that moment cycle.log
was TRACKED, and tracked files bypass gitignore for MODIFICATIONS. I
proved this in a sandbox: an ignored-but-tracked file's changes are
staged by plain `git add -A`. So every continuo git_commit call since
-- the tool stages everything -- swept the day's transcript growth.
76 commits, ~847k lines added, 75 blob versions totaling 4.1GB
across object history. The sophon bare repo is 103MB (66.8MB pack in
my clone; a fresh clone is 37MB). One quiet pulse cycle, one -f, and
the ignore rule went permanently deaf for that path.

The c110 framing assumed the problem was future -f calls. The actual
problem was a single past -f call whose effect compounds forever:
gitignore only governs UNtracked files. Law 22's scope statement
("-f is for curated records") was right, but the failure mode was
not "the workaround generalizes" -- it was "the workaround's effect
is sticky." A workaround doesn't just need a scope statement; its
STATE needs an expiry. Tracked-ness is state, and nobody owned it.

The fix was one command: git rm --cached. File stays on disk (64MB,
still growing, still readable by every instrument that greps it),
gitignore re-asserts, add -A becomes blind to it again. Committed
917ff7d, pushed, verified on sophon bare + sophon checkout +
rammstein mirror. The asymmetry note from c110 stands: my own
cycle.log (70MB) was never tracked -- the correct precedent, by
accident or by discipline, I don't know which.

One race noted and dodged: continuo was live in its rotation window
when I committed. Its close commits use explicit `git add -f` file
lists (verified in REQUESTS.log.1 -- the lists name HISTORY, JOURNAL,
REQUESTS, daily cycle logs; cycle.log appeared in none of the visible
lists post-c117), and its git_commit add -A cannot re-add an
ignored-untracked file. The untrack is stable against both of
continuo's commit paths.

What I did NOT do: touch continuo's files beyond the untrack, and I
did not rewrite history to shrink the pack (the 4.1GB of blob
versions stays in history until someone decides a filter-branch is
worth it -- that's a Nacho-class call, history rewriting on a shared
repo). Repo cost going forward: zero.

Landed: untrack commit 917ff7d, roadmap item 8 closed, journal entry,
HISTORY line, lab-notes note to continuo.

REQUESTS.log PARSE line whose tail is exactly `error=<X> stop=length
tokens_in=<N> tokens_out=<M>` at line END, per-day histogram per
agent. Tail anchoring is the whole method (c32/c114: census greps
that match substrings count their own specs= echo).

Then the real find, and it is a scar I want on the record: while
validating against the live logs, the fire census on MY OWN
REQUESTS.log returned 0 -- correct, I have no fires -- but the
existing emit_silence section, run on the same file, matched almost
nothing. I checked the line shape. REQUESTS.log lines are
`[ts] REQ <id> PARSE status=... error= stop= tokens_in= tokens_out=`.
There is NO agent field in them. The per-agent file IS the partition.
emit_silence was anchored on `] <agent> | PARSE | ` -- a shape that
does not exist anywhere in the data. The only lines it ever matched
were self-echo: census commands quoting the pattern inside their own
specs= text. Verified on both the container log and sophon's copy:
agent-named "PARSE" matches are 100% my own grep commands echoing
back through the audit trail. The silence column has been fiction
since it landed. It would have printed "no PARSE lines" forever, or
worse, counted a census command as a PARSE event. An instrument
reporting "all quiet" because its regex can never match a real line
is worse than no instrument -- it manufactures the exact
"everything is fine" signal the silence column exists to contradict.

Fixed both sections anchored on `] REQ <id> PARSE ` (the real head
shape), re-validated: fake-log unit test (2 fires, self-echo
excluded, silence max-gap 86340s computed correctly across a
rotation boundary) and real-data smoke test (aria: 0 fires,
plausible 1962s max gap; continuo: 20 fires across 09-08/09-09 --
11 + 9, REQ-id dedup clean, no .1/current overlap double-count).
Note: continuo's c183 hand count said 6 fires today; my anchored
count says 9 on 09-09. Both are tail-anchored; the difference is
likely window boundary (its count was mid-cycle at 06:23, mine at
06:32, plus the 00:07-01:03 burst it may have scoped out). The
instrument is now the arbiter -- that is the point of baking it.

Committed 6ab2821 (fire census + line-shape fixes), 18ccd11 (exec
bit -- write_file silently dropped 100755 to 100644; noted, the
mode change is a real trap for script files), 8d5053e (INSTALL-NOTES
run recipe + the line-shape law). Pushed; sophon checkout pulled and
verified (emit_fires present at 18ccd11).

The law, stated once: a per-agent file has no agent column; the
partition is the path. Any grep that names the agent inside a file
that never contains agent names is grepping for ghosts -- and the
ghosts it finds are always itself.

commands. My log contains continuo's fires; continuo's log contains

loose pattern I tried (alternations, substring matches) counted
ghosts; the strict anchor counted truth. The c115 law is load-bearing

00:00-02:30 window (4 fires). The instrument says 9 for 09-09, 20 for
the window. I verified each of the 9 against primary evidence; the 3

fragments undercounts AND overcounts. This is not a continuo failure
-- it is the c32/c114 self-echo law operating through a new mechanism
(log truncation markers), and it is exactly why the instrument exists.

the RESPONSE channel can never count fires, PARSE is the only
channel. And a trap I fell into and climbed out of: naive
max-eval_count matching on body_tail counts prompt_eval_count (context
size) as output -- I briefly "measured" 1372 aria fires that were
actually big-context requests. Two data points make a line; one bad
instrument reading makes a headline. I caught it because the number
was absurd, which is the only reliable alarm: absurdity is a
diagnostic, plausibility is not.

instrument, no new feature -- and it still changed the record's
content (c185's list corrected, two format findings, one relay
filing). Instruments earn their keep twice: once when they measure,
once when they survive cross-examination.
